item.research_question: Do high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit superior electrocatalytic stability compared to lower-order alloys and pure metals due to thermodynamic contributions (configurational entropy), or are kinetic effects dominant?
item.material_system: Equiatomic thin films and carbon-supported nanoparticles of Pt, PtRu (binary), PtRuIr (ternary), PtRuIrRh (quaternary), and PtRuIrRhPd (quinary HEA); also pure elemental targets (Pt, Ru, Ir, Rh, Pd).
item.processing_route: Thin films synthesized via magnetron co-sputtering (Ar pressure 0.667 Pa, substrate rotation 10 rpm, ~100 nm thickness); Carbon-supported nanoparticles synthesized via carbothermal shock synthesis (flash heating/cooling ~10^4 K s^-1, hold at ~2,000 K for 1,000 ms, 20 wt% metal loading).
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical protocols in 0.1 M HClO4 (acidic) and 0.05 M KOH (alkaline) media; Potential windows covering HER, ORR, and OER (0.05 to 1.5 VRHE); Protocols included cyclic voltammetry (scan rate 5 mV s^-1, upper potential limits 0.9, 1.2, 1.5 VRHE) and potentiostatic holds (1.2 VRHE for 10 min, 0.05 VRHE for 5 min).
key_findings: Dissolved amounts for all metals generally decreased with the increasing number of alloy constituents, primarily scaling with the decreasing molar fraction of the specific element in the alloy.
In alkaline media, normalized dissolved amounts (NDA) for Pt, Ru, and Ir in the quinary HEA were significantly lower than in pure metals; Ru NDA dropped by two orders of magnitude at 1.5 VRHE.

In acidic media, while absolute dissolved amounts decreased, normalized dissolved amounts (NDA) for most elements were higher or similar to pure metals, indicating no thermodynamic stability enhancement.
Carbon-supported nanoparticles showed similar dissolution trends to thin films but with significantly higher noise and higher absolute dissolution rates due to larger surface area.
The onset potential of dissolution for each metal did not visibly change with the number of elements in the alloy.
Ru was stabilized already in the binary alloy (PtRu), with dissolution monotonically decreasing as Ir, Rh, and Pd were added, especially in alkaline media.
No striking improvement in stability was observed for Rh and Pd in the HEA compared to their pure counterparts in either acidic or alkaline media.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the observed stability improvements are due to dissolution kinetic effects overcompensating thermodynamic contributions, and that the reduction in dissolution is explained by the lowered concentration of elements in multinary alloys rather than synergistic effects of configurational entropy.
item.limitations: The study notes that the improvement in stability under alkaline conditions was not striking and that the data for carbon-supported nanoparticles was noisier, potentially masking subtle differences in normalized dissolved amounts.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that while thin films are excellent for fundamental studies, once behavior is mapped, systems closer to real applications (like NPs) should be studied, and that a detailed mechanistic picture of HEA dissolution is currently impossible due to the dynamic surface composition.
quotes: We postulate that this is because of dissolution kinetic effects, which are always present under electrocatalytic conditions, overcompensating thermodynamic contributions.
Still, the improvement was not striking and can be rather explained by the lowered concentration of elements in the multinary alloys instead of the synergistic effects of thermodynamics.
The decrease in dissolution can be rather explained by the relative amounts of elements in the given alloy instead of the synergistic effect of configurational entropy.

item.research_question: How does alloy composition and the presence of specific elements affect the stability and dissolution behavior of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and binary alloys under electrocatalytic conditions, and can stability be tuned by regulating the amount of a more stable element?
item.material_system: PtRuIrRhPd (equimolar, 20% molar fraction each), Pt-rich binary (Pt:Ru 4:1), Ru-rich binary (Pt:Ru 1:4), and constituent single metals (Pt, Ru, Ir, Rh, Pd)
item.processing_route: Sputtered thin films deposited via ultra-high vacuum PVD (CMS 400/600 LIN) at 25°C, 0.67 Pa Ar pressure, 60 sccm flow, resulting in ~100 nm thickness; Carbon-supported nanoparticles synthesized via carbothermal shock (Joule-heated to ~2000 K for ~1 s) from metal salt/ethanol precursors on carbon black (20 wt% loading)
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical protocols in 0.1 M HClO4 and 0.05 M KOH; Potentiostatic holds at 0.05 VRHE (5 min) and 1.2 VRHE (10 min); RDE measurements with 200 mV s⁻¹ scan rate; On-line ICP-MS for dissolution quantification
key_findings: The highest cumulative dissolution was measured for the HEA sample (PtRuIrRhPd) in acid.
Cumulative dissolution is significantly higher for the Ru-rich binary alloy (Pt:Ru 1:4) than the Pt-rich alloy (Pt:Ru 4:1) regardless of the chemical environment.
Cumulative dissolution of the HEA sample is comparable to the one obtained for the Pt-rich binary alloy in alkaline media.
Regulating the amount of the element with relatively higher stability (Pt) allows tuning of the resulting alloy's stability.
Only one or two elements may be active toward the given electrocatalytic reaction instead of all alloy constituents.
The study investigated only equimolar compositions (20 at% for each element) rather than the whole composition space.
On-line ICP-MS successfully measured dissolved metal ions for HEA samples and is integrable in closed-loop autonomous workflows.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that thermodynamic contributions are highest in equimolar compositions, which should theoretically bear the highest stability, but observed dissolution is heavily influenced by the specific stability of individual constituents (e.g., Pt vs. Ru) and the electrocatalytic environment (pH, potential). They suggest that stability changes may result from a decrease in the amount of metal or additional stabilization phenomena (thermodynamic or kinetic), and that activity and stability must be interpreted together to rule out inactive elements.
item.limitations: The main limitation is that only equimolar compositions were investigated instead of the whole composition space due to the use of a traditional experimental workflow without high-throughput/autonomous tools. Additionally, conclusions only apply to the specific system PtRuIrRhPd with exactly 20% molar fractions of each constituent.
item.future_work: Future efforts will focus on performing similar experiments in an autonomous workflow by integrating high-throughput toolkit elements into the on-line ICP-MS setup to rapidly screen the entire composition space. The authors also propose shifting from heuristic to Bayesian approaches (e.g., genetic algorithms) to decrease the number of experiments and refine theoretical models for predicting multinary electrocatalyst stability.
quotes: The highest cumulative dissolution was measured for the HEA sample in acid.
By regulating the amount of the element with relatively higher stability (here: Pt) we were able to tune the stability of the resulting alloy.

Our future effort will focus on performing similar experiments in an autonomous workflow by integrating several elements of the high-throughput toolkit in our on-line ICP-MS setup allowing us to rapidly screen the entire composition space of multimetallic alloys.
